newsitem.title: USA: METAL PREMIUMS-Aluminum/zinc firmer, nickel stable.
newsitem.headline: METAL PREMIUMS-Aluminum/zinc firmer, nickel stable.

text.p: Metal premiums in the United States were holding up after the midsummer lull with aluminum and zinc even showing signs of firming, while nickel, tin and lead remained stable, traders said.
Premiums on western grade aluminum have edged up to 3.65 to 3.75 cents per pound over LME cash for nearby Midwest delivery, up about 0.15 cent on the lower end of the range.
Offers for next year were quoted at 3.5 to 3.75 cents per pound. Business was still fairly quiet.

Zinc premiums also edged up to 5.75 to 6.25 cents per pound over LME cash as the market awaited the next U.S. Mint tender, probably on September 17, the same day as the next government stockpile zinc sale, traders said.
"Metal remains fairly tight in the U.S. and people are expecting strong premiums from the Mint tender," a zinc merchant said.

Lead failed to live up to its promise over the summer, but some of the bigger customers have bought extra metal and this has tightened the market slightly, with premiums firm at 4.0 to 6.0 cents per pound over LME cash, traders said.
Physical nickel business was quiet but premiums were holding up at 8.0 to 12.0 cents per pound over LME cash.
Tin was also quiet with supplies adequate, though traders were keeping a close eye on LME stocks to see if they plunge below 10,000 tonnes.
The outcome later this month from the bids to buy tin on long-term contracts from the U.S. DLA government stockpile was keenly awaited.

RMT Metals, a large buyer of tin under the old, daily spot DLA sales, would need to win a big slice of the new long-term metal to continue with its U.S. tin crystallizer project to upgrade stockpiled tin into higher quality metal, market sources said.
"There was fierce competition for this tin and the DLA gets the best price, but for the winner it would be tough to make money on it," the sources said.
